column1: Why must a conductor's beat (ictus) lead the sound rather than react to it?
column2: Sound travels roughly 1 ft/ms (343 m/s, ~3 ms/meter), causing tens of milliseconds of delay across an ensemble. If the conductor reacts to sound, attacks spread out; the ictus must be the synchronization reference, not the sound.

column1: What are the three pillars that make conducting physically effective?
column2: Temporal Authority (steady, unambiguous pulse so players don't chase tempo), Visual Clarity (baton tip path must be clean and large enough to see from the back), and Physical Authority (gesture originates in the whole body—shoulders, spine, breath—not just the wrist).

column1: What is the correct baton grip mechanic, and why does a tight grip fail?
column2: Thumb and index form a loose V-cradle about 1/3 from the tip (balance point); middle/ring/pinky stabilize without squeezing; wrist stays neutral/straight. A tight grip transmits tension up the arm into the shoulder, producing a stiff, telegraphed beat and causing fatigue/injury.

column1: Define the ictus and explain why players attack on it specifically.
column2: The ictus is the exact moment the baton changes direction (sudden stop-and-reverse at the bottom of a gesture, like a ball bouncing off a floor). Players attack on this precise point of deceleration, not on the preparatory rise or the rebound afterward—because they watch the approach and predict the arrival.

column1: Why does an ambiguous, gradually-decelerating ictus cause ensemble 'mush'?
column2: Players respond to velocity change, not arm position. A gradual stop gives a range of possible attack moments instead of one unambiguous instant; with many players each guessing within that range, the result is audibly smeared rather than a clean attack.

column1: What is the rule for stepping up metronome tempo during drills, and why?
column2: Use small steps (4-5 BPM) below 80 BPM and larger steps (10 BPM) above 120 BPM, because listeners perceive tempo change by ratio: 60→80 BPM is a 33% change while 140→160 is only 14%. Equal ratio steps feel equally significant.

column1: In dynamics conducting, when must a change in volume be shown, and why?
column2: The change must be shown one beat early, in the preparatory beat or rebound, before the first note at the new level sounds—because players (bow speed/weight, air pressure) must decide their physical approach before the note is produced, not after.

column1: What distinguishes how a conductor shows dynamic level versus articulation?
column2: Size and height of the gesture show dynamic level; weight and rebound speed show articulation. Using size to show articulation (instead of level) is an invariant violation that confuses the ensemble.

column1: Why must a conductor 'reserve' gestural width early in a long crescendo (e.g., 8 bars)?
column2: Because one written dynamic step is roughly 5-8 dB and every ~10 dB sounds twice as loud, the pp-to-ff range is very large. If the gesture's size grows too early, there is no room left to show the final increase, and players will reach the target level too soon.

column1: What is the correct resting plane for standard baton beat patterns, and why does it matter?
column2: An imaginary horizontal plane roughly at sternum height. Dropping on strong beats and lifting on weak beats relative to this plane makes the pattern readable at a glance—even peripherally—by musicians who are mostly watching their own part.

column1: What is the role of the left hand in conducting, according to the core invariants?
column2: The left hand adds independent information (shaping dynamics, cueing, cutting off, targeting a section)—it does not copy or mirror the right hand's beat pattern.

column1: Why is the common advice 'conduct the future, hear the past' critical to rehearsal error correction?
column2: Because sound travel delay (~3 ms/meter) means that by the time a conductor hears a late entrance, it's already too late to fix that specific entrance—the gesture can only anticipate and correct the next one, not the one already past.
